title: The corner of the field (Mishnah Peah)
hookLine: how much to leave for the poor, and who may gather it

lines: ONE END OF THE FIELD STILL STANDING.
cards: The wheat is down across the whole field except one end. There, a strip of grain still stands, gold and untouched, as if the reapers forgot it. They didn't.
The farmer's work is done, and he's gone home. Later, people who own no field at all come with their own sickles and cut it themselves. Nobody hands it to them.
Nobody picks who gets some. It's theirs by right. The Torah asks for this strip, and the Mishnah gives it a whole tractate.
How big? And who takes it?

teach.h: PEAH: THE TORAH GIVES NO SIZE.
teach.b: The corner of the field. In Hebrew, peah. The Torah's command, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corner of thy field."
Leave it, it says, for the poor and for the stranger. It never says how much. So the Mishnah, in tractate Peah, asks.

teach.h: NO LESS THAN A SIXTIETH; NO CEILING.
teach.b: It admits the Torah set no measure, then sets a floor: no less than one sixtieth. The right amount depends on the size of the field, the number of the poor, and how good the harvest was. A floor, but no ceiling.
A big year and a crowd of hungry people should mean a bigger corner. The second question: who gathers it?
The Mishnah says the corner is given while the grain still stands, and the poor reap it themselves. The farmer doesn't cut it and hand it out to people he likes.
There are exceptions, grapes on high trellises and dates at the top of tall palms, where the owner brings the fruit down and divides it. But the rule is that the corner isn't the farmer's gift.
It belongs to the poor, and they come and take what is theirs. Near its close, the tractate turns to the one who takes.
In paraphrase: whoever takes without needing to will not leave the world before coming to need others. And whoever truly needs, and holds back from taking, will live to support others from their own.
The corner is for those who need it, and the one who takes is asked to be honest about that.

how: Jewish law treats the corner of the field as the poor's by right; where farming laws are kept in the land of Israel, some farmers still leave peah, and Jewish teachers draw on these laws when describing giving that protects the dignity of the one who receives.

games.q: what does “the corner of the field” mean?
o: the edge of a harvest left for the poor to reap
the first fruits a farmer gives to the Temple
a tenth of the crop given to the Levites

games.q: the corner of the field — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah sets the size of the corner
it says not to wholly reap the corner and never says how much. the Mishnah sets a floor.
the Mishnah says not less than one sixtieth
a floor, no ceiling: more for a big field, many poor, a good harvest.
the farmer chooses which poor people get his corner
the poor reap it themselves, while it's still standing.

games.q: you're a farmer. the harvest is in, except the corner. a poor neighbor you like is nearby, and so are strangers. what does the Mishnah say happens?
o: cut it and give it to the neighbor you like.
leave it standing; the poor come and reap it themselves.
sell it and give the money away.
games.why: the corner is given while still attached to the ground, and the poor reap it themselves. it isn't the farmer's to hand out.

practice: Think of one thing you'll have plenty of today: food in the fridge, time, money, patience.

Picture its corner, the part you could leave standing for someone else, without deciding who will get it, because that's the point of the corner. Then picture it set where someone who needs it can reach it without having to ask.

wordCard.voice: The corner of the field. Peah: the edge of the harvest left standing for the poor, at least a sixtieth, and reaped by the poor themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: corner, edge; the corner of the field left for the poor, and the name of the tractate.

carryVoice: Your line: the corner. It's theirs by right, not a favor. Go gently.

sources.q: thou shalt not wholly reap the corner of thy field
